entries.meaning: A machine that carries people or goods from place to place. ---
examples: No vehicles are allowed on the beach after dark.
The police stopped a vehicle with no license plate.
Electric vehicles are getting cheaper every year.
entries.contrast: The h is silent in American speech: VEE-uh-kuhl, not vee-HIK-ul.

entries.meaning: A road vehicle with four wheels that carries a small number of people. ---
examples: We bought a used car last spring.
There were three cars in the driveway.
I left my phone in the car.

entries.meaning: A large road vehicle built for carrying heavy loads. ---
examples: A delivery truck blocked the whole street.
He drives a truck cross-country.
Two trucks pulled into the loading dock.
entries.contrast: Americans say truck where the British say lorry.

entries.meaning: A boxy road vehicle used for carrying goods or a group of people. ---
examples: The band loaded their gear into a white van.
Delivery vans park along this block all day.
We rented a van for the move.

entries.meaning: A two-wheeled vehicle with an engine. ---
examples: He rides a motorcycle to campus.
A row of motorcycles was parked outside the diner.
She sold her motorcycle after the accident.

entries.meaning: A two-wheeled vehicle you move by pushing pedals. ---
examples: My daughter got a bicycle for her birthday.
Bicycles have to stay off the sidewalk here.
He fixed the chain on his bicycle.

entries.meaning: A bicycle, in everyday speech. ---
examples: I rode my bike to the store.
There's a rack for bikes behind the library.
Somebody stole his bike from the porch.

entries.meaning: A small vehicle you stand or sit on, moved by a foot or a small engine. ---
examples: The kid pushed his scooter up the hill.
Rental scooters are parked all over downtown.
She rides a scooter to class.

entries.meaning: A light motorbike with pedals and a very small engine. ---
examples: He got around the island on a rented moped.
Mopeds don't need a motorcycle license here.
Her moped barely goes thirty miles an hour.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, MOH-ped; not the past tense of mope, which is /moʊpt/.

entries.meaning: A three-wheeled cycle, usually for a small child. ---
examples: He pedaled his tricycle down the driveway.
Two tricycles were left out in the rain.
She's too big for a tricycle now.

entries.meaning: A short board on four small wheels that you ride standing up. ---
examples: He carried his skateboard under one arm.
Skateboards aren't allowed inside the mall.
She landed the trick and hopped off the skateboard.

entries.meaning: A heavy vehicle with big rear wheels used for farm work. ---
examples: A tractor was plowing the field at sunrise.
Two old tractors rusted behind the barn.
He climbed down off the tractor.

entries.meaning: A tall family car with sliding doors and three rows of seats. ---
examples: They traded the sedan for a minivan after the twins were born.
Three minivans pulled up for the field trip.
The minivan holds seven people.

entries.meaning: A light truck with an open cargo bed behind the cab. ---
examples: He threw the ladder in the back of his pickup.
Pickups outsell every other vehicle in this state.
Her pickup has over two hundred thousand miles on it.

entries.meaning: A car with four doors and a separate trunk. ---
examples: A gray sedan was idling at the curb.
Midsize sedans used to be the family standard.
He drives a four-door sedan.
entries.contrast: Americans say sedan where the British say saloon.

entries.meaning: A car whose roof folds down. ---
examples: We rented a convertible for the drive up the coast.
Convertibles aren't very practical in Michigan.
He put the top up on the convertible when it started raining.

entries.meaning: A long luxury car driven by a hired driver. ---
examples: A black limousine waited outside the church.
Two limousines took the wedding party to the reception.
They rode to the airport in a limousine.

entries.meaning: A small car whose rear door lifts up along with the window. ---
examples: A little red hatchback squeezed into the space.
Hatchbacks hold more than you'd think.
She loaded the groceries into the hatchback.

entries.meaning: A four-wheeled cart pulled by animals or by hand. ---
examples: The horses pulled a heavy wagon full of hay.
Covered wagons carried settlers west.
He hauled his toys around in a little red wagon.

entries.meaning: A small wheeled container you push or pull. ---
examples: My shopping cart had a bad wheel.
Carts are stacked by the store entrance.
He wheeled the cart out to the parking lot.
entries.contrast: A store cart in the US is a trolley in Britain.

entries.meaning: A wheeled seat for pushing a small child around. ---
examples: She folded the stroller and put it in the trunk.
Strollers have to be checked at the gate.
The baby fell asleep in the stroller.
entries.contrast: American stroller; the British say pushchair or pram.

entries.meaning: A flat board or frame on runners for sliding over snow. ---
examples: The kids dragged a sled up the hill.
Plastic sleds were sold out everywhere.
He steered the sled around a tree.
entries.contrast: Americans say sled; the British usually say sledge.

entries.meaning: A large sled pulled by horses or reindeer. ---
examples: They took a sleigh ride through the snowy woods.
Two horse-drawn sleighs waited by the lodge.
The sleigh had bells on the harness.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like slay.

entries.meaning: A wheeled passenger vehicle pulled by horses. ---
examples: A horse-drawn carriage circled the park.
Carriages line up near the hotel on summer evenings.
They rode home in an open carriage.
entries.contrast: In Britain a carriage is also a railroad car; Americans say car for that.

entries.meaning: A vehicle or trailer fitted out to sleep and cook in. ---
examples: They spent the summer living out of a camper.
Campers have to park in the lower lot.
He backed the camper into the campsite.

entries.meaning: A tracked machine with a wide blade for pushing earth. ---
examples: A bulldozer leveled the lot in an afternoon.
Two bulldozers sat idle behind the fence.
The bulldozer pushed the rubble into a pile.

entries.meaning: A small warehouse vehicle with two prongs that lift heavy pallets. ---
examples: A forklift moved the pallets into the truck.
You need training to drive one of these forklifts.
The forklift beeped as it backed up.

entries.meaning: A truck with a blade in front that clears snow off roads. ---
examples: A snowplow came through around four in the morning.
The city sent out every snowplow it had.
Snowplows piled the snow at the end of the driveway.
entries.contrast: American spelling snowplow; the British write snowplough.

entries.meaning: A motor vehicle on skis and a track, for driving over snow. ---
examples: They crossed the frozen lake on a snowmobile.
Snowmobiles are loud but they're fast.
He rents out snowmobiles every winter.

entries.meaning: A truck that pulls away broken or illegally parked cars. ---
examples: We waited an hour for the tow truck.
A tow truck hauled the wreck off the shoulder.
Two tow trucks showed up at the same time.
entries.contrast: Tow rhymes with go and sounds like toe, never like cow.

entries.meaning: A red truck that carries firefighters, ladders and hoses. ---
examples: A fire truck went by with its siren on.
Three fire trucks blocked the intersection.
The kids waved at the fire truck.

entries.meaning: A truck whose bed tips up to pour out its load. ---
examples: A dump truck dropped a load of gravel in the driveway.
Dump trucks rumbled past the site all day.
The dump truck raised its bed and unloaded.

entries.meaning: A long car that carries a coffin to a funeral. ---
examples: The hearse pulled slowly out of the church lot.
Two black hearses led the procession.
He restored an old hearse and drives it to car shows.

entries.meaning: A streetcar drawing power from an overhead wire. ---
examples: A trolley runs from the harbor to the zoo.
The trolleys stop running at eleven.
We hopped on the trolley at Fifth Street.
entries.contrast: In Britain a trolley is a shopping cart, not a streetcar.

entries.meaning: The powered railroad engine that pulls a train. ---
examples: A diesel locomotive pulled forty cars.
Steam locomotives are kept running at the railroad museum.
The locomotive let out a long whistle.

entries.meaning: An enclosed freight car with sliding side doors. ---
examples: The kids counted boxcars as the train went by.
A boxcar sat abandoned on a siding.
They loaded grain into the boxcar.

entries.meaning: An airplane driven by jet engines. ---
examples: A private jet was parked at the far end of the field.
Fighter jets flew over the stadium.
The jet climbed steeply after takeoff.

entries.meaning: A light aircraft that flies without an engine. ---
examples: A glider circled silently over the ridge.
Gliders are towed into the air by a small plane.
He learned to fly in a glider first.

entries.meaning: A small airship with no rigid frame inside. ---
examples: A blimp floated over the stadium during the game.
Blimps are used mostly for advertising now.
The blimp carried a camera crew.

entries.meaning: An airplane built to take off from and land on water. ---
examples: A seaplane dropped us at the fishing lodge.
Seaplanes are the only way into some of these lakes.
The seaplane taxied up to the dock.

entries.meaning: A large building where aircraft are kept and repaired. ---
examples: The plane was towed into the hangar.
Two mechanics were working in the hangar.
Old hangars line the far side of the field.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like hanger, the thing you hang a coat on, but ends in -ar.

entries.meaning: The main body of an aircraft, where passengers and cargo ride. ---
examples: The fuselage was built in sections.
Investigators found a crack in the fuselage.
Both fuselages were shipped by rail to the plant.

entries.meaning: A set of spinning blades that pushes an aircraft or boat forward. ---
examples: The propeller started turning slowly.
The plane has two propellers, one on each wing.
A rope got caught in the boat's propeller.

entries.meaning: The wheels and struts an aircraft lands and rolls on. ---
examples: The landing gear came down with a thump.
They found a hydraulic leak in the landing gear.
The pilot raised the landing gear right after takeoff.

entries.meaning: The business and practice of flying aircraft. ---
examples: He's had a career in aviation since the seventies.
Aviation fuel costs more than it used to.
She studies aviation at a school in Florida.

entries.meaning: A narrow open boat pointed at both ends, moved with a paddle. ---
examples: We rented a canoe for the afternoon.
Two canoes were tied up at the dock.
He tipped the canoe over getting in.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: kuh-NOO.

entries.meaning: A narrow covered boat you sit inside and paddle with a double blade. ---
examples: She keeps a kayak on the roof of her car.
Kayaks are lighter than canoes.
He rolled the kayak upright again.

entries.meaning: A boat driven by the wind in its sails. ---
examples: A small sailboat crossed in front of us.
Sailboats dotted the bay all afternoon.
He built the sailboat himself.

entries.meaning: A small boat moved with oars. ---
examples: There's an old wooden rowboat behind the cabin.
Rowboats rent for ten dollars an hour.
We took the rowboat out to the island.

entries.meaning: A small powerful boat that pushes and pulls larger ships. ---
examples: A tugboat nudged the freighter into the slip.
Two tugboats worked the harbor that morning.
The tugboat blew its horn twice.

entries.meaning: A boat driven by an engine. ---
examples: A motorboat roared past and rocked our canoe.
Motorboats aren't allowed on this lake.
He tied the motorboat to the dock.

entries.meaning: A long flat boat for hauling freight on rivers and canals. ---
examples: A coal barge moved slowly down the river.
Barges line up above the lock.
The barge was pushed by a single towboat.

entries.meaning: A ship or truck built to carry liquid in bulk. ---
examples: An oil tanker ran aground off the coast.
Tankers deliver fuel to the station twice a week.
The tanker was empty on the return trip.

entries.meaning: A ship that carries cargo rather than passengers. ---
examples: A rusty freighter was tied up at the pier.
Freighters come through the canal day and night.
The freighter carried grain to Egypt.
entries.contrast: The eigh sounds like ay: FRAY-tur.

entries.meaning: A very small boat, often carried by a larger one. ---
examples: We rowed the dinghy ashore.
Two dinghies were lashed to the deck.
The dinghy had a tiny outboard motor.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: DING-ee.

entries.meaning: A short pole with a flat blade, held in the hands to move a canoe. ---
examples: He dropped his paddle in the water.
There are two paddles under the seat.
She dug the paddle in and turned the canoe.

entries.meaning: A long pole with a blade that rests in a fitting on a rowboat. ---
examples: One oar slipped out of the lock.
He pulled hard on both oars.
The oars were stored under the dock.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like or and ore.

entries.meaning: A large sheet of cloth that catches the wind to move a boat. ---
examples: The wind filled the sail.
They lowered the sails before the storm hit.
One sail was torn along the bottom edge.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sale.

entries.meaning: The tall upright pole that holds a boat's sails. ---
examples: He climbed halfway up the mast.
The boat has two masts.
Lightning split the mast in half.

entries.meaning: A flat blade at the back of a boat or plane used for steering. ---
examples: The rudder was jammed and we couldn't turn.
Large ships have two rudders.
He nudged the rudder and the bow swung left.

entries.meaning: The main body of a boat or ship that sits in the water. ---
examples: The hull was scraped and repainted.
Fiberglass hulls are lighter than wooden ones.
Water was coming in through a crack in the hull.

entries.meaning: A small boat kept on a ship for use in an emergency. ---
examples: Passengers were sent to the lifeboats.
Each lifeboat holds thirty people.
They lowered the lifeboat into the water.

entries.meaning: A padded vest that keeps a person afloat in water. ---
examples: Everyone in the boat has to wear a life jacket.
There are four life jackets in the front compartment.
Her life jacket was too big.

entries.meaning: A round part that turns on an axle and lets a vehicle roll. ---
examples: The front wheel was bent in the crash.
All four wheels need to be balanced.
A shopping cart wheel kept sticking.

entries.meaning: The wheel a driver turns to point the car left or right. ---
examples: Keep both hands on the steering wheel.
The steering wheel was hot from sitting in the sun.
Older steering wheels were much bigger than today's.

entries.meaning: The rubber ring fitted around a wheel. ---
examples: I got a flat tire on the way home.
All four tires are worn down.
Check the pressure in the spare tire.
entries.contrast: American spelling tire; the British write tyre.

entries.meaning: The part of a vehicle that slows it down or stops it. ---
examples: He slammed on the brakes.
The rear brake is squealing again.
New brakes cost me four hundred dollars.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like break.

entries.meaning: The panel of dials and controls in front of a driver. ---
examples: A warning light came on in the dashboard.
He keeps his sunglasses on the dashboard.
Newer dashboards are basically one big screen.

entries.meaning: The arm with a rubber blade that clears rain off a windshield. ---
examples: Turn on the wipers, it's starting to rain.
One wiper is leaving streaks.
The wipers couldn't keep up with the downpour.

entries.meaning: The bar across the front or back of a car that takes small impacts. ---
examples: Someone dented my rear bumper in the lot.
Both bumpers are plastic on this model.
He put a sticker on the bumper.

entries.meaning: The body panel curving over a wheel. ---
examples: The front fender is rusting out.
He hammered the dent out of the fender.
Both fenders were repainted.
entries.contrast: Americans say fender; the British say wing on a car and mudguard on a bike.

entries.meaning: A lamp at the front of a vehicle that lights the road ahead. ---
examples: Turn your headlights on, it's getting dark.
One headlight is burned out.
The headlights of an oncoming car blinded me.

entries.meaning: A red lamp at the back of a vehicle. ---
examples: A cracked taillight got him pulled over.
I could just see her taillights in the fog.
The left taillight doesn't work.

entries.meaning: The flashing light that shows which way a vehicle is about to turn. ---
examples: He changed lanes without using his turn signal.
Both turn signals were blinking too fast.
Put your turn signal on before you slow down.
entries.contrast: Americans say turn signal; the British say indicator.

entries.meaning: A turn signal, in casual American speech. ---
examples: You left your blinker on for a mile.
His blinkers stopped working after the accident.
Hit the blinker before you turn.

entries.meaning: The part of the exhaust system that quiets the engine noise. ---
examples: His muffler is shot and you can hear him coming.
The shop replaced the muffler for ninety dollars.
Rusted mufflers are common on cars this old.
entries.contrast: Americans say muffler; the British say silencer.

entries.meaning: The burned gas an engine pushes out. ---
examples: Black exhaust poured out of the old bus.
Never run the engine in a closed garage; the exhaust can kill you.
You could smell the exhaust from the highway.
entries.contrast: The h is silent and exh- sounds like igz-: ig-ZAWST.

entries.meaning: The pipe at the back of a vehicle where exhaust comes out. ---
examples: Steam was coming from the tailpipe.
The truck has two chrome tailpipes.
Something is rattling near the tailpipe.

entries.meaning: The set of gears that sends engine power to the wheels. ---
examples: The transmission is slipping in second gear.
A new transmission costs more than the car is worth.
Automatic transmissions have gotten much smoother.

entries.meaning: The rod that a pair of wheels turns on. ---
examples: He broke an axle going through the pothole.
A truck like that has three axles.
The rear axle was leaking oil.

entries.meaning: A cylinder that damps the bouncing of a vehicle's springs. ---
examples: The front shock absorbers are leaking.
One shock absorber was completely worn out.
New shock absorbers made a huge difference.

entries.meaning: The part that makes an electric spark to fire the fuel in a cylinder. ---
examples: A fouled spark plug was making it misfire.
He changed all six spark plugs himself.
The new spark plugs cost four dollars each.

entries.meaning: The tube in an engine where the piston moves and the fuel burns. ---
examples: It's a six-cylinder engine.
One cylinder wasn't firing at all.
The cylinders were rebored during the rebuild.

entries.meaning: The shaft that turns the pistons' up-and-down motion into spinning. ---
examples: The crankshaft has to be perfectly balanced.
He found a worn bearing on the crankshaft.
Broken crankshafts usually mean a new engine.

entries.meaning: The older part that mixes fuel and air before it enters the engine. ---
examples: The carburetor needs cleaning.
Old motorcycles have twin carburetors.
Fuel injection replaced the carburetor in the eighties.
entries.contrast: American spelling carburetor; the British write carburettor.

entries.meaning: A flat seal that stops fluid leaking between two engine parts. ---
examples: He blew a head gasket on the highway.
Rubber gaskets dry out over time.
The mechanic replaced the gasket and the leak stopped.

entries.meaning: The part driven by the engine that charges the battery. ---
examples: A dead alternator left me stranded.
Alternators usually last well over a hundred thousand miles.
The shop tested the alternator for free.

entries.meaning: The small motor that turns an engine over to get it running. ---
examples: The starter just clicks and nothing happens.
He replaced the starter in the parking lot.
Starters on these cars are hard to reach.

entries.meaning: The switch and system that start a vehicle's engine. ---
examples: Put the key in the ignition and turn it.
The ignition is worn out and the key sticks.
Push-button ignitions have replaced keys on newer cars.

entries.meaning: The pedal that makes a vehicle go faster. ---
examples: She pressed the accelerator and pulled onto the highway.
His foot slipped off the accelerator.
The accelerator felt stiff in the cold.

entries.meaning: The control that regulates how much fuel and air reach an engine. ---
examples: He eased off the throttle going into the turn.
The pilot pushed the throttles forward.
A stuck throttle is dangerous.

entries.meaning: The lever a driver moves to change gears. ---
examples: The gearshift sits between the front seats.
He rested his hand on the gearshift.
Old trucks had gearshifts on the steering column.

entries.meaning: The metal or plastic cover over the center of a wheel. ---
examples: I lost a hubcap hitting the curb.
All four hubcaps were missing.
The hubcap rolled halfway down the street.

entries.meaning: The metal ring of a wheel that the tire sits on. ---
examples: He bent a rim on a pothole.
The car came with alloy rims.
You can't drive on a bare rim.

entries.meaning: The grooved rubber pattern on the outside of a tire. ---
examples: There's almost no tread left on these tires.
Snow tires have deeper tread.
The mechanic measured the tread with a gauge.
entries.contrast: The ea sounds like the e in bed: TRED.

entries.meaning: A panel in a car's roof that opens to let in air and light. ---
examples: She opened the sunroof on the drive home.
The sunroof leaks when it rains hard.
Sunroofs are standard on the higher trim.

entries.meaning: The strap that holds a person in a vehicle seat. ---
examples: Buckle your seat belt before we go.
The rear seat belts were never used.
His seat belt saved his life.

entries.meaning: A bag that inflates instantly in a crash to protect a passenger. ---
examples: The airbag went off and broke his glasses.
This model has eight airbags.
A faulty airbag led to a huge recall.

entries.meaning: The padded top of a car seat that supports the head. ---
examples: Adjust the headrest so it's level with your ears.
The rear headrests fold down for visibility.
He leaned back against the headrest and closed his eyes.

entries.meaning: The numbered metal plate that identifies a vehicle. ---
examples: A witness got the license plate number.
License plates have to be renewed every year here.
The rear license plate was covered in mud.
entries.contrast: Americans write license and say license plate; the British write licence and say number plate.

entries.meaning: The small storage box in a car's dashboard on the passenger side. ---
examples: The registration is in the glove compartment.
He rooted around in the glove compartment for a napkin.
Both glove compartments in that van lock.

entries.meaning: The container in a vehicle that holds its fuel. ---
examples: The gas tank holds about fourteen gallons.
We filled the gas tank before leaving town.
Rusted gas tanks are a known problem on that model.
entries.contrast: Americans say gas tank; the British say petrol tank.

entries.meaning: The extra tire kept in a car in case one goes flat. ---
examples: The spare tire is under the floor of the trunk.
Don't drive over fifty on that spare tire.
Some new cars don't come with spare tires at all.

entries.meaning: The mirror above the windshield that shows the road behind. ---
examples: He checked the rearview mirror before braking.
An air freshener hung from the rearview mirror.
Newer rearview mirrors dim automatically at night.

entries.meaning: A liquid added to an engine's water so it will not freeze or boil. ---
examples: Add some antifreeze before winter.
There was green antifreeze pooled under the car.
Antifreeze is poisonous, so keep it away from pets.

entries.meaning: The bar a rider holds and steers a bicycle or motorcycle with. ---
examples: He hung a bag from the handlebars.
The handlebars need to be raised a little.
She gripped the handlebars and pushed off.
entries.contrast: Usually used in the plural, handlebars, even for the one bar.

entries.meaning: One of the thin rods running from the center of a wheel to its rim. ---
examples: A spoke snapped on the back wheel.
He wove a card through the spokes.
The spokes need to be tightened evenly.
entries.contrast: Spelled and said exactly like spoke, the past tense of speak.

entries.meaning: The seat on a bicycle, motorcycle or horse. ---
examples: The saddle is too high for her.
Gel saddles are easier on long rides.
He raised the saddle an inch.

entries.meaning: The small folding leg that props a bike upright when parked. ---
examples: Put the kickstand down before you let go.
The kickstand is bent and won't hold the bike.
Racing bikes don't come with kickstands.

entries.meaning: A toothed wheel that a chain runs over. ---
examples: The chain jumped off the sprocket.
Worn sprockets make the chain skip.
He swapped in a bigger rear sprocket.

entries.meaning: The rubber balloon inside a tire that holds the air. ---
examples: I patched the inner tube twice already.
Carry a spare inner tube on long rides.
Both inner tubes had slow leaks.
entries.contrast: Americans say TOOB; the British say TYOOB.

entries.meaning: A small piece that shines back light from headlights so a bike is seen. ---
examples: The red reflector fell off the back of his bike.
State law requires reflectors on the pedals.
A reflector is not a substitute for a real light.

entries.meaning: A person riding a bicycle. ---
examples: A cyclist passed us going uphill.
Cyclists use the shoulder on this road.
The cyclist signaled and turned left.

entries.meaning: A person driving a car, in news and official language. ---
examples: Motorists were warned to avoid the bridge.
A motorist stopped to help.
The city is asking motorists to slow down in school zones.

entries.meaning: Someone employed to drive another person's car. ---
examples: Her chauffeur waited outside the restaurant.
The company keeps two chauffeurs on staff.
He worked as a chauffeur for twenty years.
entries.contrast: French spelling: ch sounds like sh, and the -eur ending is just -ur.

entries.meaning: A trip in a vehicle, especially one someone gives you. ---
examples: Can you give me a ride to the airport?
It's a two-hour ride on the bus.
She offered rides to anyone going downtown.

entries.meaning: A bad vehicle crash, or what is left of the vehicle after one. ---
examples: There was a wreck on the interstate this morning.
Two wrecks were towed off before rush hour.
He walked away from the wreck without a scratch.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: REK, the same sound as the start of wrench.

entries.meaning: A long car with a rear door and extra cargo space behind the back seat. ---
examples: Their old station wagon had fake wood on the sides.
Station wagons mostly gave way to SUVs.
We fit all six of us in the station wagon.

entries.meaning: A car built for competing on a track. ---
examples: The race car spun out on the last lap.
Race cars have no doors that open normally.
He built a race car in his garage.

entries.meaning: A car pulled along by a moving cable, up a hill or across a valley. ---
examples: We rode the cable car up the mountain.
San Francisco still runs its old cable cars.
The cable car stopped halfway up.

entries.meaning: A train that runs on a single rail, usually raised above the ground. ---
examples: The monorail connects the terminals.
Two monorails run through the park.
We took the monorail to the hotel.

entries.meaning: The crew car at the end of an old freight train. ---
examples: The kids waved at the red caboose.
Cabooses disappeared from American railroads in the eighties.
An old caboose sits on display outside the depot.

entries.meaning: A small motor craft you ride sitting or standing on the water. ---
examples: He rented a jet ski for an hour.
Jet skis are banned in the cove.
She fell off the jet ski twice.

entries.meaning: A boat built to be lived in rather than traveled in. ---
examples: They live on a houseboat year-round.
Houseboats line the far side of the marina.
The houseboat barely moves.

entries.meaning: A small boat with a powerful engine, built to go fast. ---
examples: A speedboat pulled the water-skier.
Speedboats churn up the whole lake.
He opened up the speedboat once we cleared the buoys.

entries.meaning: A large fabric bag lifted by heated air, carrying a basket underneath. ---
examples: A hot-air balloon drifted over the valley at sunrise.
Dozens of hot-air balloons went up at the festival.
He proposed in a hot-air balloon.

entries.meaning: The long ridge along the bottom of a boat that keeps it steady. ---
examples: The keel scraped a sandbar.
Racing sailboats have deep keels.
They repaired the keel over the winter.

entries.meaning: The back end of a boat or ship. ---
examples: He stood at the stern and watched the wake.
The name is painted across the stern.
Both sterns were damaged in the collision.

entries.meaning: A floating marker anchored in water to guide boats. ---
examples: A red buoy marks the channel.
Don't swim past the buoys.
The buoy rang softly in the swell.
entries.contrast: Americans say BOO-ee; the British say it like boy.

entries.meaning: A small round window in the side of a ship. ---
examples: She looked out the porthole at the harbor.
The cabin has two portholes.
Salt spray covered the porthole.

entries.meaning: The shaft with lobes that opens and closes an engine's valves. ---
examples: A worn camshaft made the engine tick.
This engine has two camshafts.
The camshaft turns at half engine speed.

entries.meaning: A heavy disc on an engine that keeps it turning smoothly. ---
examples: The flywheel was cracked and had to be replaced.
Flywheels store energy as they spin.
He resurfaced the flywheel during the clutch job.

entries.meaning: The spinning rod that carries power from the transmission to the wheels. ---
examples: The driveshaft snapped and we coasted to a stop.
Four-wheel-drive trucks have two driveshafts.
He greased the driveshaft joints.

entries.meaning: The part of the exhaust system that cleans up harmful gases. ---
examples: Someone stole the catalytic converter right off the car.
Catalytic converters contain valuable metals.
A bad catalytic converter will fail you at inspection.

entries.meaning: The thick clamped wires used to start a car from another car's battery. ---
examples: Do you have jumper cables in the trunk?
He hooked up the jumper cables and the engine turned over.
A good set of jumper cables costs about twenty dollars.
entries.contrast: Almost always used in the plural; the British call them jump leads.

entries.meaning: One of the nuts that hold a wheel onto a vehicle. ---
examples: Loosen the lug nuts before you jack up the car.
One lug nut was rusted solid.
Tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern.

entries.meaning: The hinged panel at the back of a pickup or wagon that folds down. ---
examples: They sat on the tailgate eating sandwiches.
The tailgate wouldn't latch anymore.
Both tailgates were dented.

entries.meaning: The pattern of bars across the front of a vehicle that lets air in. ---
examples: A rock cracked the plastic grille.
You can tell the model by the grille.
Bugs were stuck all over the grille.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like grill, the thing you cook on, but keeps the final e.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is driving a large truck long distances. ---
examples: A trucker stopped and gave us a jump.
Truckers fill this rest stop every night.
He's been a trucker for fifteen years.

entries.meaning: An arrangement where people share one car for a regular trip. ---
examples: She joined a carpool to save on gas.
The carpool picks him up at seven.
Two carpools leave from this lot every morning.

entries.meaning: A vehicle that rides on a cushion of air over water or flat ground. ---
examples: A hovercraft crossed the channel in half an hour.
Two hovercraft were tied up at the ramp.
The hovercraft threw spray in every direction.
entries.contrast: The plural is usually hovercraft, unchanged, like aircraft.

entries.meaning: The narrow board people walk across to get on or off a boat. ---
examples: She hurried down the gangplank.
The crew pulled up the gangplank.
Both gangplanks were slick with rain.

entries.meaning: A boat driven by a steam engine, often with a paddle wheel. ---
examples: A steamboat still runs tours on the river.
Steamboats carried cotton down the Mississippi.
The steamboat blew its whistle at the landing.

entries.meaning: A small engine clamped to the back of a boat. ---
examples: He yanked the cord on the outboard motor.
Outboard motors are easy to take off and store.
The outboard motor quit halfway across.

entries.meaning: An old-style airplane with two sets of wings, one above the other. ---
examples: A yellow biplane did loops over the field.
Biplanes were standard in the First World War.
He restored a 1930s biplane.

entries.meaning: A large truck used for carrying furniture to a new home. ---
examples: A moving van was double-parked outside.
Moving vans are booked solid at the end of August.
They loaded the moving van in the rain.

entries.meaning: A tiny open racing car with no roof or doors. ---
examples: He drove a go-kart for the first time at eight.
Go-karts top out around forty miles an hour.
The go-kart spun into the tires.

entries.meaning: A cycle with a single wheel, ridden for balance and show. ---
examples: He rode a unicycle down the hall.
Unicycles are harder than they look.
She learned to ride a unicycle in one summer.

entries.meaning: The rubber belt that keeps an engine's moving parts turning together. ---
examples: The timing belt snapped and wrecked the engine.
Timing belts should be changed around a hundred thousand miles.
Replacing the timing belt costs about eight hundred dollars.

entries.meaning: The screw-on canister that cleans grit out of an engine's oil. ---
examples: Change the oil filter every time you change the oil.
Oil filters cost only a few dollars.
He couldn't get the old oil filter loose.

entries.meaning: The rubber strip on a wiper arm that sweeps the windshield. ---
examples: The wiper blade left a streak right at eye level.
Wiper blades should be replaced about once a year.
A cracked wiper blade scratched the glass.

entries.meaning: The pedal a driver presses to slow the car down. ---
examples: He stomped on the brake pedal.
The brake pedal felt spongy.
Both brake pedals in the driving-school car work.

entries.meaning: The pedal a driver presses to speed the car up. ---
examples: She eased off the gas pedal.
The gas pedal stuck halfway down.
Rubber covers on gas pedals wear through fast.
entries.contrast: Americans say gas pedal; the British say accelerator.

entries.meaning: The pair of small extra wheels that keep a child's bike upright. ---
examples: We finally took the training wheels off.
A set of training wheels comes with the bike.
He rode with training wheels until he was six.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural; the British say stabilizers.

entries.meaning: The part that pushes gasoline from the tank to the engine. ---
examples: A dead fuel pump left the car stranded.
Fuel pumps usually sit inside the gas tank.
Replacing the fuel pump took the shop two days.

entries.meaning: The frame on top of a vehicle for carrying bulky loads.
examples: They strapped the kayak to the roof rack.
Roof racks hurt your gas mileage.
The roof rack whistled at highway speed.
